newsitem.title: USA: Galileo flies by Jupiter's moon Ganymede.
newsitem.headline: Galileo flies by Jupiter's moon Ganymede.

text.p: The Galileo space probe on Friday flew within 160 miles (260 km) of Jupiter's largest moon Ganymede, taking pictures of its icy, fault-ridden surface.

Scientists at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory here said the unmanned spacecraft flew over Ganymede's north pole at 3 p.m. EDT (1900 GMT) on Friday. The mission was Galileo's second flyby of Ganymede -- the largest moon in the solar system -- since arriving in the Jovian atmosphere in December.

Galileo was collecting new pictures of two regions on the moon's surface, Uruk Sulcus and Galileo Regio, that it took images of in June. This will allow scientists to create a three-dimensional view of Ganymede's surface.

National Aeronautics and Space Administration scientists were anxious to study the patterns of the fissures and cracks that riddle the moon's surface and also settle a controversy over whether the moon has an internally generated magnetic field.
"It would make it the first moon in the solar system known to have a self-generated magnetic field of its own," said Mary Beth Murrill, spokeswoman for JPL.
"It's a characteristic that until now we thought that only planets had. This can help us determine how the Earth's own magnetic field is generated," she added.
Data from the latest flyby will be stored onboard Galileo and transmitted to Earth over two months starting on Monday.
The next flyby for the space probe is on Nov. 4 when it will take pictures of the heavily cratered third moon of Jupiter, Callisto.
Scientists say the planned December flyby of another Jupiter moon, Europa, will spark even more interest.
"People are particularly looking forward to the Europa flyby in December," Murrill said.

"Given the results from the recent discussion about the possibility of life on Mars and the potential for liquid water on Europa people are excited to find out whether there really is liquid water on Europa and what that could mean for the potential of a life-bearing environment there," she said.
Galileo was launched aboard the space shuttle Atlantis on Oct. 18, 1989, and was almost half way through its two-year mission in the Jovian atmosphere.
